entries.title: Pompano en papillote
entries.summary: Antoine's dish of pompano baked in a sealed paper parcel over a sauce of shrimp and crabmeat in a white wine velouté. The parcel puffs with steam in the oven and is cut open at the table.
entries.guest: Pompano en papillote is Antoine's classic: a rich Gulf fish baked in a paper parcel with shrimp and crab in a white wine sauce. Ours, the Gulf Fish en Papillote, uses banana leaf.

paras: Pompano en papillote, said POM-puh-noh ahn pah-pee-YOHT, is a fillet of pompano baked in a sealed paper parcel with a sauce of shrimp and crabmeat bound in a white wine velouté, a stock sauce thickened with a pale roux. In a hot oven the parcel swells with steam and reaches the table taut and browned at the edges, to be cut open before the guest in a rush of butter, wine and seafood.
It is one of the plates that made Antoine's famous.

Pompano here means the Florida pompano, a flat-sided, silvery fish of the jack family from the warm Gulf and south Atlantic. Its firm, white, rich flesh has a fine flake and enough natural fat to stay moist in a closed parcel. Fish of 450 g to 1.4 kg (1 to 3 lb) are usual, sold whole: look for bright eyes, red gills and a clean smell of the sea.

Make the sauce first and chill it, so it sits on the fish instead of running. Many classic recipes poach the fillets briefly in fish stock and white wine, then build the velouté from that liquid, so the oven has only to heat and puff the parcel. For four portions, cook 40 g (1.5 oz) each of butter and flour without colour, let the roux cool for a minute, then whisk in 500 ml (about 2 cups) of the hot liquid a ladle at a time and simmer 15 to 20 minutes, until it coats a spoon thickly.
Stir in a reduction of shallot and dry white wine, then 225 g (8 oz) each of cooked, chopped shrimp and lump crabmeat. Some cooks enrich it with a yolk off the heat. Season, then chill until set.

Butter a heart of baking parchment about 40 cm (16 inches) across for each portion. Spoon sauce onto one half, lay on a fillet of 150 to 180 g (5 to 6 oz), raw or lightly poached, and cover it with more sauce, then fold the paper over and crimp the edge tight; the entry on en papillote teaches the fold. Bake at 200 to 220°C (392 to 428°F) until the parcel puffs and browns: about 12 to 15 minutes for a raw fillet, 8 to 10 for one already poached, which needs only to heat through. The fish is done at 63°C (145°F) at its thickest point.

Inside the sealed paper, the sauce and the fish's juices turn to steam, which cooks the fish gently and inflates the parcel. Opening it at the table shows the guest the puff and releases the aroma with the fish at its moistest. Cut across the top and fold the edges away from the guest, so the steam rises clear of faces.

A parcel that leaks lets the steam out, so the paper never puffs and the fish dries: crimp tighter. A sauce that runs and scorches was too thin or not chilled. Because the paper hides the fish, overcooking is the commonest fault: cut fillets to one thickness and time each batch.

Antoine's credits Jules Alciatore, the founder's son, with the dish. The house story is that he created it for a dinner honouring Alberto Santos-Dumont, the Brazilian balloonist, and that the puffed paper recalled a balloon. Tellings usually place it around 1901, the year Santos-Dumont flew his airship round the Eiffel Tower and became famous across the world. Tell it as the house's story.

Our Gulf Fish en Papillote carries the idea forward: the day's Gulf fish wrapped in banana leaf rather than paper, with Louisiana crab, tomato, Castelvetrano olives, sorghum and Marcona almonds, so it steams in its own juices. The entry on en papillote teaches our dish in full. Learn the fish at lineup, and ask there whether the parcel is opened at the table.

When a guest mentions Antoine's pompano, link the two in a sentence: the same sealed parcel, another wrapper and another fish. Never call ours pompano unless lineup names it as the day's fish. Warn the guest that the steam is hot, and send questions about the shellfish or the almonds to the kitchen.

faults.cause: The crimp leaked and the steam escaped.
faults.fix: Fold in small, tight, overlapping pleats all the way round and twist the point shut.

faults.cause: The sauce was too thin or went on warm, so it ran out to the paper.
faults.fix: Cook the velouté thick and chill it until set before building the parcel.

faults.cause: Fillets of uneven thickness, or a bake timed by guesswork.
faults.fix: Cut fillets to one thickness, time each batch and probe a test parcel.

faults.fault: A limp, wrinkled parcel at the table
faults.cause: It waited at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, and the steam inside cooled.
faults.fix: Send it the moment it leaves the oven and open it at once.

brennans.how: The day's Gulf fish is wrapped in banana leaf, not paper, with Louisiana crab, tomato, Castelvetrano olives, sorghum and Marcona almonds, so it steams in its own juices. Ask at lineup whether it is opened at the table, and warn the guest about the steam.

cards.front: What is pompano en papillote?
cards.back: Antoine's dish of pompano baked in a sealed paper parcel with a sauce of shrimp and crabmeat in a white wine velouté, cut open at the table.

cards.front: What kind of fish is pompano, and why does it suit a parcel?
cards.back: A flat-sided, silvery Gulf fish of the jack family, with firm, rich white flesh whose natural fat keeps it moist in a closed parcel.

cards.front: What sauce binds the shrimp and crab in the classic version?
cards.back: A white wine velouté: fish stock thickened with a pale roux, with a reduction of white wine and shallot, sometimes enriched with a yolk.

cards.front: Why is the sauce chilled before the parcel is built?
cards.back: A cold, set sauce stays on the fish instead of running to the edges, where it would leak or scorch.

cards.front: How is the paper parcel sealed?
cards.back: A heart of buttered parchment is folded over the fish and crimped in small, tight, overlapping pleats, with the point twisted shut so no steam escapes.

cards.front: Why does the parcel puff in the oven?
cards.back: The sauce and the fish's juices turn to steam and the sealed paper traps it; the swelling shows the inside is at full steam.

cards.front: What oven and time suit a parcel of pompano?
cards.back: A hot oven, 200 to 220°C (392 to 428°F), until the parcel puffs and browns: about 12 to 15 minutes for a raw fillet, 8 to 10 for a poached one. The fish is done at 63°C (145°F).

cards.front: Why is the parcel cut open at the table?
cards.back: The guest sees the puff and meets the first rush of aroma with the fish at its moistest; the edges fold away so the steam rises clear of faces.

cards.front: What story does Antoine's tell about the dish?
cards.back: Jules Alciatore created it for a dinner honouring the Brazilian balloonist Alberto Santos-Dumont, and the puffed parcel recalled a balloon. Tell it as the house's story.

cards.front: What goes wrong when a parcel leaks?
cards.back: The steam escapes, the paper never puffs and the fish dries out; crimp tighter and overlap every pleat.

cards.front: How does our Gulf Fish en Papillote echo Antoine's dish?
cards.back: The same sealed parcel, but the day's Gulf fish is wrapped in banana leaf with Louisiana crab, tomato, olives, sorghum and Marcona almonds.

cards.front: A guest asks whether our Gulf Fish en Papillote is pompano. What do you say?
cards.back: Only if lineup names pompano as the day's fish; otherwise name the day's Gulf fish, wrapped in banana leaf, and send shellfish and almond questions to the kitchen.

questions.q: Why is pompano prized for cooking in a sealed parcel?
questions.answer: Its firm, rich white flesh stays moist
distractors: Its pink flesh keeps its colour
Its soft flesh melts into the sauce
Its dark flesh stands up to strong sauce
questions.why: Pompano's white flesh carries enough natural fat to stay moist in gentle steam, and it is firm enough to hold its shape under the sauce.

questions.q: Which sauce binds the shrimp and crabmeat in the classic pompano en papillote?
questions.why: A velouté is stock thickened with a pale roux; finished with white wine it suits seafood and sets firm when chilled.

questions.q: Why do cooks chill the sauce before building the parcel?
questions.answer: So it stays put on the fish
distractors: So the fish cooks more slowly
So the paper browns more evenly
So the shrimp stay raw until served
questions.why: A thick, cold sauce stays where it is spooned; a warm, thin one runs to the paper's edge, where it leaks and scorches.

questions.q: What makes the paper parcel puff up in the oven?
questions.answer: Steam trapped by the sealed paper
distractors: Butter foaming up under the fish fillet
questions.why: The sauce and the fish's juices turn to steam, and a tight crimp keeps it in, so the paper inflates like a small balloon.

questions.q: Antoine's story says the dish was created to honour which guest?
distractors: John D. Rockefeller, the oil magnate
Bienville, the founder of New Orleans
questions.why: The house tells that Jules Alciatore made it for a dinner honouring Santos-Dumont, the puffed paper recalling a balloon; it is told as the house's story.

questions.q: At what temperature is the fish inside the parcel done?
questions.why: Fish is cooked through at 63°C (145°F); because the paper hides it, cooks time by thickness and probe a test parcel.

questions.q: What wraps the fish in the Brennan's Gulf Fish en Papillote?
questions.why: Brennan's wraps the day's Gulf fish in banana leaf rather than paper; the leaf holds the steam just as well and adds a faint grassy aroma.

entries.title: Creole turtle soup
entries.say: As it reads: Creole turtle soup.
entries.summary: New Orleans' dark, thick turtle soup: turtle meat simmered with a brown roux, the trinity, tomato, stock and Worcestershire, finished with sherry, lemon and chopped hard-boiled egg. A Creole answer to the clear turtle soups of old banquets.
entries.guest: Creole turtle soup is a dark, rich soup of turtle meat, thickened with a brown roux and finished with sherry and egg. Ours is 100 per cent turtle meat, as the menu says.

paras: Creole turtle soup is a thick, dark brown soup of finely chopped turtle meat. A brown roux, flour cooked in fat until it smells of toasted nuts, gives body and a roasted depth; the trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, with garlic, tomato, stock, herbs and Worcestershire sauce, builds the flavour; and the turtle's gelatine gives a rich, lip-coating body. Dry sherry, lemon and chopped hard-boiled egg finish it, often with spinach or parsley.

For about 3 litres (about 3 quarts): 900 g (2 lb) turtle meat, a roux of 225 g (8 oz) each of fat and flour, 2 litres (about 2 quarts) of brown stock with 500 ml (about 2 cups) of the turtle cooking liquid, 400 g (14 oz) chopped tomato and 450 g (1 lb) of the trinity. A brown roux thickens less than a pale one, so a dark soup takes more of it.

Simmer the turtle meat in salted water with an onion and a bay leaf for 1 to 2 hours, until tender; chop it finely and keep the liquid. Cook a medium-brown roux in oil, lard or clarified butter in a heavy pot, stirring without stopping, for 25 to 35 minutes, until it is the colour of milk chocolate; the roux ladder teaches the stages. Add the trinity, which stops the browning, soften it for 5 to 8 minutes, then add the garlic.

Stir in the tomato, then add the stock and the turtle liquid, cool or barely warm, a ladle at a time, whisking so the roux takes it smoothly. Add the turtle, bay, thyme, Worcestershire and a little hot sauce, and keep it at a lazy simmer, 85 to 95°C (185 to 203°F), for 45 minutes to an hour, skimming the fat, until it coats a spoon. Off the heat, add lemon and sherry and season; scatter egg and parsley over each bowl. Hold it at 57°C (135°F) or above, the Food Code's hot holding figure.

Turtle soup was a banquet dish long before it was Creole. The green turtle soup of London's great City dinners was often served clear, as a consommé, a broth clarified until it is transparent, with Madeira or sherry, though thick versions were made too. Philadelphia's snapper soup, from freshwater snapping turtle, is thickened and served with sherry, a cousin of the Creole soup. New Orleans made its soup thick, dark and spiced as a rule.

Turtle was always dear, so cooks stretched it. Mock turtle soup, an English invention, uses calf's head for the same gelatinous body and holds no turtle at all. Many turtle soups still stretch the turtle with veal or beef, so a menu that prints 100 per cent turtle makes a real promise.

Black specks or an acrid smell in the roux mean it has scorched, and the whole pot will taste bitter: start again. A soup that tastes flat usually wants salt, lemon or sherry rather than more spice. Add the egg at the end: stirred in early, it breaks to crumbs and greys.

Turtle soup has been eaten in Louisiana since the 1700s, and the old houses each keep a famous version: Arnaud's, Commander's Palace, Mandina's and Brennan's among them. Commander's Palace is run by another branch of the Brennan family. Sea turtles are protected now, and New Orleans soups use freshwater snapping turtle.

Our Turtle Soup has its own entry. In short, the menu prints 100% turtle meat, finished with brown butter spinach, grated egg and aged sherry, and the turtle is snapping turtle; which kind, and who supplies it, are questions for the chef.

In many old dining rooms the server offers a splash of sherry from a cruet, a small pouring bottle, so each guest sets their own level. At Brennan's, whether the sherry goes in at the kitchen, at the pass, the counter where plates leave the kitchen, or at the table is a lineup question. Tell a guest avoiding alcohol that sherry is in the bowl, and never promise it cooks off. Describe the taste rather than the animal: rich, meaty and savoury, like a deep stew. If a guest eyes the courtyard fountain, smile and say it first: the soup is not the courtyard turtles, who are family. Allergen and dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

ratios.label: Turtle meat
ratios.value: 900 g (2 lb) for about 3 litres (about 3 quarts) of soup

ratios.label: Trinity
ratios.value: 450 g (1 lb) of onion, celery and green pepper, about two parts onion to one each of the others

faults.cause: The roux scorched: black specks and an acrid smell.
faults.fix: Throw the roux out and make a new one; nothing hides scorched flour.

faults.cause: The stock went in all at once, or hot stock met a hot roux.
faults.fix: Add cool or barely warm stock a ladle at a time, whisking; strain if lumps remain.

faults.fault: Stringy meat and a greasy, cloudy soup
faults.cause: It boiled hard instead of simmering.
faults.fix: Keep a lazy simmer and skim the fat as it rises.

faults.cause: The egg went in too early and broke up.
faults.fix: Add the chopped egg at the end, over each bowl.

brennans.how: The menu prints 100% turtle meat, so no veal or beef stretches it; the turtle is snapping turtle, finished with brown butter spinach, grated egg and aged sherry. Which kind of snapping turtle, the supplier and where the sherry goes in are questions for the chef and lineup.

cards.front: How is sherry offered at the table in many old houses?

questions.q: How was the famous banquet turtle soup of London often served?

questions.q: Philadelphia's snapper soup and today's New Orleans turtle soups share which turtle?
questions.why: Snapper soup is named for the freshwater snapping turtle, and New Orleans soups, ours included, use it too, since sea turtles are protected.

questions.q: What does mock turtle soup use in place of turtle?
questions.why: Calf's head gives the same rich, gelatinous body that made turtle soup prized, at a fraction of the cost.

questions.q: What does a menu promise when it prints 100 per cent turtle meat?
questions.answer: No veal or beef stretches the turtle
distractors: The turtle was caught that very morning
The soup has no roux in it
The turtle is a sea turtle
questions.why: Many turtle soups pad the turtle with veal or beef; the phrase says the meat in the bowl is all turtle.

Parmesan and a swirl of basil oil

questions.q: A cook sees black specks in a brown roux and smells something acrid. What should happen next?
questions.answer: Discard it and make a new roux
distractors: Add more flour to cover the taste
Pour in all the stock to stop it
questions.why: Scorched flour turns the whole pot bitter, and no seasoning hides it, so the only fix is a fresh roux.

questions.q: A guest who avoids alcohol asks about the turtle soup. What should the server do?
questions.answer: Tell them sherry is in the soup
distractors: Say the alcohol all cooks away
Say nothing, as the splash is small
Promise the kitchen will leave it out
questions.why: Aged sherry finishes the soup, and cooking never removes all the alcohol, so the guest hears it before ordering; a server never promises it cooks off or can be left out.

questions.q: What finishes the Brennan's Turtle Soup, as the menu describes it?
questions.answer: Brown butter spinach, grated egg and aged sherry
distractors: Sliced lemon, chopped parsley and a dry Madeira
Filé powder, sliced green onion and white rice
Garlic croutons, grated Parmesan and a swirl of cream
questions.why: The menu prints brown butter spinach, grated egg and aged sherry over 100% turtle meat; where the sherry goes in is a lineup question. Filé and rice belong to gumbo.

entries.title: Café brûlot
entries.summary: Burnt coffee: brandy and orange liqueur flamed in a bowl with sugar, cinnamon, cloves and orange and lemon peel, then hot coffee ladled in. A New Orleans tableside ritual credited to Antoine's, and the flavour behind our Café Brûlot Coffee Cake.
entries.guest: Café brûlot is New Orleans' flaming coffee: brandy, citrus peel and spice set alight, then hot coffee poured in. Our Café Brûlot Coffee Cake carries its coffee, citrus and spice.

paras: Café brûlot, said ka-FAY broo-LOH, means burnt coffee, from the French brûler, to burn. Brandy, usually with a little orange liqueur, is warmed in a wide bowl with sugar, cinnamon, cloves and strips of orange and lemon peel, then set alight. Once the spice and peel have scented the flaming spirit, hot, strong coffee is ladled in, the flame dies down, and the drink is served in small cups.

It matters because it is one of the city's great tableside rituals: an after-dinner coffee that is also a show, and part of the memory a guest takes home. At Brennan's it reaches the guest in another form, a coffee cake named for it, so a server needs to know both the drink and why the cake carries its name.

The brûlot set is a wide metal bowl, often silver, over a small burner, with a long-handled ladle and demitasse cups, the small cups used for strong coffee. For six to eight cups: 120 ml (4 fl oz) brandy, 30 ml (1 fl oz) orange liqueur, 25 g (2 tbsp) sugar or a few cubes, a cinnamon stick, 8 to 12 cloves, a strip of lemon peel, and an orange peeled in one long spiral and studded with cloves. Have 750 ml (about 3 cups) of hot, strong coffee ready before anything is lit.

With the burner still unlit, put the sugar, cinnamon, loose cloves and lemon peel in the bowl and add the brandy and orange liqueur, measured first in a small jug. Then light the burner low to warm them, and light the warm spirit with a long match, stirring gently to melt the sugar. Now the theatre: hold the clove-studded orange spiral up on a fork over the bowl, lift flaming brandy in the ladle and pour it slowly down the peel, so the flame runs along the spiral and draws the oil from the peel. Ladle the coffee in gradually until the flame dies, then ladle the drink into cups, leaving the spice and peel behind.
The rules for any flame at the table, from measuring the spirit before lighting to keeping a lid in reach, have their own entry, and so does tableside service.

Chicory coffee is the New Orleans base: roasted, ground chicory root blended with dark-roast coffee, which brings a roasty, gently bitter, chocolatey depth and a smooth body that stands up to brandy and spice. Brew it stronger than for an ordinary cup, because the spirit and sugar dilute it. Its cousins are the other warm, spirited coffees, such as Irish coffee, which add the spirit without the fire.

Spirit that will not light is too cold: warm it in the bowl first so its vapour can catch. A flame that leaps high means too much spirit or a bowl left too long on the burner; measure first and keep the heat low. A bitter drink comes from white pith left on the peel or coffee that boiled. A thin, sweet drink means the coffee was weak.

Tradition credits Antoine's, where Jules Alciatore, the founder's son, is said to have created café brûlot diabolique, the devilish version, in the late nineteenth century. The flaming bowl became a fixture of the long New Orleans dinner and has been served in several of the old houses, Arnaud's among them. At Brennan's today it is on no menu as a drink: the house carries its flavours in a cake instead. Tell the origin as tradition: like most famous drinks, its first night is not on record.

The drink itself is not on our current list. Brennan's borrows its flavours for the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake, a sweet starter at breakfast and lunch: a chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake with pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche. Sell it as the coffee's flavours, not the flame, and suggest a cup of our chicory coffee alongside.

If a guest asks for café brûlot, say plainly that the drink is not on today's menus and offer it only if the house confirms it. Offer instead the coffee cake named for it and a cup of our chicory coffee. Tell the story as Antoine's tradition, never as a Brennan's invention. Allergy and dietary questions about the cake, nuts included, go to the service note and the kitchen.

cards.front: What does café brûlot mean?
cards.back: Burnt coffee, from the French brûler, to burn: the spirit is set alight before the coffee goes in.

cards.front: What goes into the bowl before it is lit?
cards.back: Brandy, often with orange liqueur, sugar, a cinnamon stick, cloves and strips of orange and lemon peel.

cards.front: In what order is café brûlot built?
cards.back: Spirits, sugar and spice are warmed and lit first, flaming brandy runs down the orange spiral, and hot coffee goes in last as the flame dies.

cards.front: What is the long orange spiral for?
cards.back: One peel studded with cloves, held over the bowl while flaming brandy runs down it; the flame travels the spiral and draws out the citrus oil.

cards.front: Why is chicory coffee the New Orleans base?
cards.back: Roasted chicory root blended with coffee brings a roasty, chocolatey depth and smooth body that stand up to brandy and spice.

cards.front: Why is the coffee brewed stronger than usual?
cards.back: The brandy, liqueur and sugar dilute it, and a weak coffee makes a thin, sweet drink.

cards.front: Which house does tradition credit with café brûlot?
cards.back: Antoine's, where Jules Alciatore, the founder's son, is said to have created café brûlot diabolique in the late nineteenth century.

cards.front: Why might the brandy refuse to light?
cards.back: It is too cold to give off enough vapour; warm it gently in the bowl first.

cards.front: How does Brennan's carry café brûlot today?
cards.back: In the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake: chicory coffee and chocolate cake, pecans, a spiced citrus glaze and crème fraîche. The drink is not on today's menus.

cards.front: A guest asks for café brûlot at Brennan's. What do you say?
cards.back: That the drink is not on today's menus, so it is offered only if the house confirms it; then offer the coffee cake named for it and a cup of our chicory coffee.

cards.front: What makes up a brûlot set at the table?
cards.back: A wide metal bowl, often silver, over a small burner, a long-handled ladle and demitasse cups, the small cups used for strong coffee.

cards.front: Why is the spirit measured into the bowl before the burner is lit?
cards.back: So no bottle is ever poured near a flame: the brandy and liqueur go in from a small jug first, then the burner is lit low to warm them.

questions.q: What does the word brûlot in café brûlot point to?
distractors: Brewing, from an old word for coffee
Brown, from the colour of the coffee
questions.why: Brûlot comes from brûler, to burn: the spirit is set alight in the bowl before the coffee goes in.

questions.q: When does the coffee go into the brûlot bowl?
questions.answer: Last, after the spirit is lit
distractors: Never: it is served on the side
questions.why: The flaming spirit is scented with spice and peel first; the coffee goes in last and the flame dies down.

questions.q: What is the long spiral of orange peel studded with?
questions.why: Cloves studded into the peel scent the flaming brandy that runs down the spiral and on into the coffee.

questions.q: What does chicory bring to New Orleans coffee?
questions.why: Roasted chicory root adds a gently bitter, chocolatey depth and a smooth body that stand up to the brandy and spice.

questions.q: Which restaurant does tradition credit with café brûlot?
questions.why: Tradition credits Jules Alciatore at Antoine's with café brûlot diabolique in the late nineteenth century.

questions.q: The brandy in the brûlot bowl will not light. What is the likely cause?
questions.why: Cold spirit gives off too little vapour to catch; warming it gently in the bowl lets it light.

questions.q: How does a guest meet café brûlot at Brennan's today?
questions.answer: As the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake
distractors: As a flaming drink at the table
As a cocktail at the bar
As an ice cream for dessert
questions.why: The drink is not on our list; the coffee cake carries its flavours, chicory coffee, chocolate and a spiced citrus glaze.

questions.q: How does the brandy reach the brûlot bowl?
questions.answer: Measured from a small jug, before anything is lit
distractors: Poured from the bottle into the flaming bowl
Splashed over the coffee once it is in the cups
Added to the coffee pot before it is brewed
questions.why: Measuring first keeps the bottle away from any flame: the spirit goes into the cold bowl, then the burner warms it and a long match lights it.

entries.title: Soufflé potatoes
entries.summary: Pommes soufflées: thin, even slices of potato fried twice, first in cooler oil to cook them, then in hot oil so they puff into hollow golden pillows. A classic of the old New Orleans houses, often served with béarnaise.
entries.guest: Soufflé potatoes are thin slices of potato fried twice, so they puff into crisp, hollow pillows. The old houses serve them with béarnaise for dipping.

paras: Soufflé potatoes, pommes soufflées in French, are thin slices of potato that puff in the fryer into crisp, golden, hollow pillows. They are fried twice: first in cooler oil to cook them through, then in very hot oil, where the water inside flashes to steam and blows the slice apart into two crisp skins with air between them. Salted and served at once, they are light and fragile.

They matter because they are a test. A slice cut unevenly, too thick or too thin, a potato carrying too much sugar or oil a few degrees too cool, and the slice stays flat. A cook who sends out a basket of evenly puffed soufflé potatoes has mastered slicing, oil temperature and timing at once, which is why chefs use them to judge a fry cook.

Choose a mature, floury potato such as a russet: high starch sets a firm skin, and low sugar stops it browning before it puffs. Potatoes kept in cold storage, below about 7°C (45°F), turn some starch to sugar, so avoid them. Square off the peeled potato and cut lengthwise slices about 3 mm (1/8 inch) thick on a mandoline, a flat slicer with an adjustable blade, every slice the same, then trim them to neat ovals. Some cooks rinse off the surface starch and others never wash the slices; every cook dries them thoroughly.

Two fryers run side by side. In the first, at about 150°C (302°F), fry the slices a few at a time for 4 to 6 minutes, keeping the oil moving over them, until they are cooked through, limp and blistered but not coloured. Lift them onto a rack. This stage is done ahead, and the cooled slices wait for service.

To order, drop them into the second fryer at 190 to 200°C (374 to 392°F). The good ones swell within seconds; fry them a minute or two more to crisp and colour, drain on a rack, salt and serve at once.

The first fry cooks the starch and dries each face into a thin skin while the centre stays moist. In the hot second fryer that moisture turns to steam faster than it can escape, the skins hold it, and the slice inflates. Any crack or thin spot lets the steam out.

Not every slice puffs, even in practised hands, so cooks fry more than they need and keep the flat ones off the plate. Flat slices were uneven, cracked, or cut too thick or too thin. Slices that brown before they puff come from a sugary potato or a first fry that ran too hot. Slices that puff and then collapse came out before the skins had crisped. A puffed slice softens within minutes, so they are fried to order and carried straight out.

The legend says they were found by accident in France on the day in 1837 when the railway from Paris to Saint-Germain-en-Laye opened. The royal party was late, so the chef, Collinet, pulled his half-fried potatoes from the oil; when the guests arrived he plunged them back into hot oil and they puffed. The details change with the teller, from who was late to the year, so tell it as legend. The same tradition credits Collinet with béarnaise.
New Orleans kept them. Antoine's, Arnaud's and Galatoire's have long served soufflé potatoes, often with béarnaise for dipping, and guests order them to taste the old city.

Soufflé potatoes are not on Brennan's current menus, so a guest who asks hears the story. One who wants crisp fried potatoes can be offered the Brabant Potatoes (bra-BAHNT), a breakfast and lunch side of cubed potatoes fried golden and tossed in butter with garlic and parsley; confirm the house finish at lineup. Wherever soufflé potatoes are served, they go to the table the moment they leave the fryer, with the béarnaise beside them. Warn the guest that the first bite lets out hot steam.

ratios.label: Slice thickness
ratios.value: About 3 mm (1/8 inch), every slice the same

ratios.label: First fry
ratios.value: About 150°C (302°F) for 4 to 6 minutes, cooked through with no colour

ratios.label: Second fry
ratios.value: 190 to 200°C (374 to 392°F): puffed in seconds, crisp in a minute or two

temps.label: First fry, to cook the slices
Second fry, low end, to puff them
Cold storage below this turns starch to sugar

faults.cause: Uneven or cracked slices let the steam escape; slices too thick never form two skins, and slices too thin crisp before they puff.
faults.fix: Cut every slice about 3 mm (1/8 inch) on a mandoline and handle them gently.

faults.cause: A potato carrying too much sugar, or a first fry that ran too hot.
faults.fix: Use a mature, floury potato kept out of cold storage, and keep the first oil near 150°C (302°F).

faults.cause: They left the second fryer before the skins crisped.
faults.fix: Fry a minute or two after the puff, until crisp and golden.

faults.fault: Soft, chewy slices at the table
faults.cause: They waited after frying and the steam inside condensed.
faults.fix: Fry to order and send them straight out.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907)

cards.front: What are soufflé potatoes?
cards.back: Pommes soufflées: thin, even potato slices fried twice so they puff into crisp, hollow, golden pillows.

cards.front: Why are soufflé potatoes fried twice?
cards.back: The cooler first fry cooks the slice and sets a skin on each face; the hot second fry turns the moisture inside to steam, which inflates it.

cards.front: How thick are the slices cut?
cards.back: About 3 mm (1/8 inch), every slice the same, so each cooks and puffs at the same rate.

cards.front: Which potato suits soufflé potatoes, and why?
cards.back: A mature, floury potato low in sugar, such as a russet: the starch sets a firm skin and low sugar stops it browning before it puffs.

cards.front: What oil temperature suits the first fry?
cards.back: About 150°C (302°F), for 4 to 6 minutes, until the slices are cooked, limp and blistered but not coloured.

cards.front: What oil temperature makes them puff?
cards.back: 190 to 200°C (374 to 392°F); the good slices swell within seconds, then crisp in a minute or two.

cards.front: Why does not every slice puff?
cards.back: A crack, a thin spot or an uneven edge lets the steam escape, so the slice stays flat; cooks fry more than they need.

cards.front: What does a slice that browns before it puffs tell you?
cards.back: The potato carries too much sugar, perhaps from cold storage, or the first fry ran too hot.

cards.front: What legend explains how soufflé potatoes were found?
cards.back: In 1837, at the opening of the railway to Saint-Germain-en-Laye, a late royal party made the chef refry half-cooked potatoes, which puffed. Tell it as legend.

cards.front: Where in New Orleans are soufflé potatoes a tradition, and with what sauce?
cards.back: At Antoine's, Arnaud's and Galatoire's, often served with béarnaise for dipping.

cards.front: Why are soufflé potatoes called a test of a fry cook?
cards.back: They show every fault at once: uneven slicing, the wrong potato, oil a few degrees off or poor timing all leave the slices flat.

cards.front: A Brennan's guest asks for soufflé potatoes. What do you say?
cards.back: They are not on our menus, so tell the story, then offer the Brabant Potatoes, a breakfast and lunch side of cubed potatoes fried golden with garlic, butter and parsley; confirm the house finish at lineup.

questions.q: What does the second, hotter fry do to a soufflé potato?
distractors: Cooks the starch for the first time
Melts a coating of butter inside
questions.why: The first fry cooks the slice and sets its skins; the hot oil of the second flashes the moisture to steam, which the skins trap.

questions.q: How thick should soufflé potato slices be cut?
questions.why: Thin enough to cook through and puff, thick enough to hold two skins apart; every slice the same so they behave alike.

questions.q: At about what temperature does the first fry run?
questions.why: The first fry must cook the slices through without colour; the puff comes later, in oil at 190 to 200°C (374 to 392°F).

questions.q: Which potato gives the best chance of a good puff?
distractors: A potato kept in the fridge
questions.why: Starch sets a firm skin and low sugar keeps the slice pale until it puffs; cold storage turns starch to sugar.

questions.q: A few slices in a batch stay flat. What usually caused it?
distractors: The oil was changed that morning
The slices were salted after frying
The basket was shaken during frying
questions.why: The puff depends on two sealed skins trapping steam; a crack or a thin spot lets it out, and the slice stays flat.

questions.q: Slices turn brown before they puff. What is the likely cause?
questions.answer: Too much sugar in the potato
distractors: A first fry that ran too cool
Too little salt on the slices
A basket that was too full
questions.why: Sugar browns fast in hot oil, so a sugary potato colours before it can puff; a mature, floury potato stays pale longer.

questions.q: The legend of soufflé potatoes ties them to which event?
questions.answer: The opening of a French railway in 1837
distractors: A banquet for Santos-Dumont at Antoine's
questions.why: The legend says a royal party arrived late for the railway opening to Saint-Germain-en-Laye, and the refried potatoes puffed.

questions.q: Which sauce do the old New Orleans houses often serve with soufflé potatoes?
questions.why: Antoine's, Arnaud's and Galatoire's have long served soufflé potatoes with béarnaise, the warm butter sauce, for dipping.
